# **Decision Log**

This document tracks the reasoning and decisions made while working on the test, so it can be reused directly for the "dataset/schema/approach and why" and "key trade-offs" sections of the README later. It will keep being updated as the project moves forward. Also it helps me keep track of things to do 😂

# **1\. Task overview**

What's being asked:&nbsp;

Build a structured document extraction system (LLM/VLM/OCR+LLM) plus an evaluation harness that proves the system is accurate not just a demo on a clean document, but proven to work on messy real-world documents, that knows when to be unsure (abstain), and that can be reasoned about in terms of quality, latency, and cost.

* **What's weighted most heavily (from the rubric):**

* **Evaluation rigor** trustworthy ground truth, failures understood by kind (not just counted), results comparable across versions

* **Extraction quality** accurate on messy documents, handles multi-page/tables/cross-section fields, no hallucination

* **LLM/VLM engineering** a sound approach, reliable validated output, meaningful confidence and abstention

* **Production-readiness** cost/latency visible, one measured optimization, resilience to bad output

* **Agentic development** effective use of an AI coding agent \+ one custom extension actually used

* **Code quality & communication**

# **2\. Key decisions (made before building)**

**2.1 Document type: receipt**

**Why:** Has a mix of simple lookup fields (vendor name, date) and fields that require reasoning (line items table, total \= subtotal \+ tax)  matches the brief's requirement for "simple lookups vs reasoning across sections." Ground truth is also easy to build manually since fields are limited and well-defined.&nbsp;

**Alternatives considered and rejected:**

**Contract** too ambiguous to schema within the time available, fields like "party's role" require heavy reasoning

**ID document** privacy concerns if using real data

**2.2 Dataset source: Own physical receipts (self-photographed)**

**Why:** The brief explicitly states "**your own scans count most.**" Physical receipts photographed by hand naturally carry real-world messiness (skew, uneven lighting, faded thermal print) without needing to be artificially engineered. Also i already have quite a bit of them lying around and in my gallery so it makes it easier for me too 😂

**Things to note**: All receipts collected are Indonesian-market receipts currency is Rupiah throughout, dates are consistently DD/MM/YYYY. What actually mixes is the language on the receipt itself (some printed in Bahasa Indonesia, some in English, e.g. imported goods stores, international chains, or English-template invoices) currency and date format are NOT mixed. This is being kept intentionally because:

useful axis for eval analysis: does accuracy differ between receipts with Indonesian vs English field labels?

Possible future extension (not in current scope): may add USD or other-currency receipts with different date conventions later to stress-test normalization further. Current dataset is IDR/DD-MM-YYYY only — the schema and prompt should still include a currency field so this extension doesn't require a schema change later, but normalization logic only needs to handle one currency and one date format for now.

Target count: 20-30 own receipts (might increase) with intentional variation and possibly more taken from the internet

**2.3 Extraction approach: VLM directly (Gemini via Google AI Studio)**

**Why over OCR+LLM:**

Single API call per document → faster to build and debug within a tight timeline

More robust to skewed/dirty scans no accumulated OCR error noise feeding into the LLM

Gemini Flash is free and explicitly recommended in the brief

Gemini handles Indonesian text reasonably well (to be validated on 2-3 initial samples)

**Why not an agentic/multi-step pipeline:**

Single-page documents with a relatively flat structure don't need complex multi-step reasoning

A single well-designed call is cheaper, faster, and easier to explain and debug in a live-code session

**BUT** OCR+LLM might still used as one optimization experiment in the Production section, not as the main path so the trade-off can still be demonstrated without adding complexity to the core architecture

**2.4 Language/stack: Python**

Why: Already familiar, speeds up development within the tight (2-3 day) window.

# **3\. Execution Plan**

**Step 1 — Collect & digitize receipts**  
Target 20-30 physical receipts with deliberate variation: some clean/straight, some skewed, 1-2 in low light, at least one faded thermal print, at least one long receipt (may need multi-shot). Keep the Indo/English label mix. Save as receipt\_001.jpg etc. Jot rough notes (store, total, date) while shooting — speeds up Step 8 later.

**Step 2 — Setup Environment and Gemini API access**  
Setup Git, coding agent, env, etc. Get/refresh API key from Google AI Studio, install google-generativeai, store key in .env. Run one trivial test call (send an image, ask for a free-text description) before building anything structured — just to confirm auth, image handling, and rate limits work.

**Step 3 — Define field schema**  
Most critical step — everything downstream depends on it. Write the Pydantic model: simple fields (vendor\_name, transaction\_date, receipt\_number), computed fields (subtotal, tax, total), nested line\_items (description, qty, unit\_price, amount), currency (future-proofing). Decide how confidence is attached per field (separate \_confidence field vs {value, confidence, reason} wrapper) and which fields can be None/abstained vs required.

**Step 4 — Extraction prompt \+ core function**  
One function: image path in, Gemini call with explicit schema instructions (use JSON mode if available), parse to Pydantic. Prompt must explicitly forbid guessing ("null if unclear, don't invent") and require confidence \+ short reason per low-confidence field. On parse failure, retry once with the error message fed back into the prompt. Test with mocked responses first, independent of live API.

**Step 5 — Resilience & error handling**  
Explicit rubric criterion, not optional. Handle: API/network failures (retry with backoff, mark as extraction\_failed rather than crashing the batch), repeated parse failures after retry (return partial result flagged as error, never silently return empty-looking-valid data), and corrupt/unreadable files (validate before sending). System must clearly distinguish "low-confidence success" from "hard failure."

**Step 6 — Sample test & iterate**  
Run on 2-3 representative samples (easy one, mixed-language one, blurry/skewed one) before the full batch. Check manually: Indonesian labels read correctly? Rupiah thousand-separator parsed as float correctly (not misread as decimal)? Date conversion DD/MM/YYYY → ISO correct (not swapped to MM/DD)? Fix prompt now if there's a consistent error pattern — cheaper to fix on 3 documents than after the full run.

**Step 7 — Build ground truth** *(can run in parallel with Steps 4-6 once Step 3 is done)*  
Manually label all receipts in the same schema as model output, reading from the original receipts — never from model output, to avoid anchoring bias. Include at least one receipt with a genuinely missing/unreadable field to test abstention later.

**Step 8 — Wrap extraction as an API service**  
Turn the function into an HTTP endpoint (FastAPI), including a batch endpoint that accepts multiple documents. Log per-request cost (tokens) and latency — needed later for Step 12's before/after comparison.

**Step 9 — Build the eval harness**  
Compare API output vs ground truth: per-field precision/recall, numeric tolerance for amounts, row-alignment method for line items, and a failure-kind breakdown (wrong value / hallucinated / wrongly abstained / misread).

**Step 10 — Dockerize**  
docker compose up serves the API (Step 9); docker compose run \--rm eval runs the harness (Step 10\) against that API and writes scorecard \+ per-document results to a mounted output directory.

**Step 11 — Full batch run, scorecard, version comparison**  
Run all receipts, review the failure breakdown, then run a second variant (e.g. revised prompt) and compare both scorecards side by side — this is your "catch a regression" demonstration.

**Step 12 — Apply one optimization, measure impact**  
Pick one (e.g. image resize before sending), measure before/after using the cost/latency numbers already logged in Step 8\.

**Step 13 — Build the custom agentic-dev extension**  
An actual small tool you used, not just a README mention (e.g. a script/skill that scaffolds ground truth templates or assists labeling).

**Step 14 — Write README \+ final commit**  
Pull from the decision log: dataset/schema/approach+why, architecture, trade-offs, eval results, agentic-dev note, next steps. Commit everything including the scorecard from a real run.

**Step 2 — Setup Environment and Gemini API access**

Initialized git repository, created a Python virtual environment, and set up base dependencies (google-generativeai, python-dotenv, pydantic) via requirements.txt. Created .env (untracked, holds the actual API key) and .env.example (tracked, template only) to keep secrets out of version control. Connected the local repository to a private GitHub remote (Receipt\_Extraction) for submission.

Settled on using gemini-3.6-flash (since it is the cheapest). Also the google-generativeai which was in the requirements.txt turns out to be deprecated and thus changed to google-genai.&nbsp;

Ran a trivial connection test sending receipt\_001.jpeg to Gemini and requesting a free-text description, to validate authentication and image handling before building structured extraction. The model successfully described the contents of a test receipt image. Environment, SDK, and model choice are now correct and ready to move to the next step
